title: Operators, Strings & Conditionals (Theory)
summary: Run short pieces of code for arithmetic, comparison and logical operators and precedence, string indexing, slicing and methods, and if / elif / else, and check the results predicted on the slides.

operators.summary: Run the operator examples from the slides as one-line programs. Check the value and type of expressions, // and %, comparisons and ranges, short-circuiting with and / or, precedence and compound assignment. At the end, run a leap-year program that uses all of these operators (the solution to Session 2, Lab 4).
steps: 8 / 2 is the float 4.0 even though both operands are integers, and "8" + "2" is the str 82. Predict the value and type before running it.
Seen with repr, raw still has its leading and trailing spaces. The numeric addition gives 15, and the string concatenation gives 123.
7 // 3 is 2, 7 % 3 is 1 and 7 ** 3 is 343. -7 // 3 rounds down, so it is -3, not -2.
Answers to the exercise: 3 hours 5 minutes, and 7 groups of 4 with 1 student left. Check that quotient × divisor + remainder gives back the original values 185 and 29.
Comparisons return True/False. The string "85" and the integer 85 are not equal, so input must be converted before comparing.
<= includes the endpoint and < excludes it. The two results differ at 0 and 100, and for 101 both are False.
and is True when both are true, or is True when at least one is true, and not reverses the value.
Both print False and there is no error. The first condition is False, so 10 / n and text[0] are never evaluated (short-circuiting).
14, 20, -4, 4. ** binds more tightly than unary -, so -2 ** 2 is -4. and comes before or, so the first expression is True; with parentheses it is False.
Compound assignments run in written order: 85, and then (5 + 3) × 2 = 16.
A leap-year test that combines %, ==, and, or and not in one expression. After the Year: prompt you get 2000: Leap year, 1900: Not a leap year. It is worked through in detail in Session 2, Lab 4.

string_basics.summary: Run string indices and negative indices, IndexError, slicing and reversing, immutability, strip, lower, upper, replace, split and in, string joining and f-strings, and the receipt example. At the end, run a string processing program that combines them (the solution to Session 2, Lab 1).
steps: Length 6, first character P (index 0), text[2] is t, and the negative indices -1 and -2 count from the end: n, o.
With length 6, the valid indices are 0 to 5. text[5] is n, and text[6] is IndexError: string index out of range.
In a one-character string the first and last characters are the same (True). An empty string has no valid index, so it is an IndexError.
Py, thon, Pyth, Pto, nohtyP, Python. The stop index is not included, and a slice past the end, [:99], is cut at the end without an error.
Answers to the exercise: YTH, PYT, HON, YHN, NOHTYP. When start and stop are equal the result is an empty string, shown by repr as ''.
Building a new string gives Jython. Strings are immutable, so assigning to text[0] gives TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment.
Methods return a new string. split() makes the list ['Hello', 'Python'], and in is case-sensitive: True, False.
A text-cleaning pipeline: strip affects only the ends, while replace also changes the space in the middle, giving hello-python. The original raw is unchanged.
+ joins and * repeats. To join a number with +, you need str(). After normalizing the input, " YES " equals "yes" (True).
The receipt example: the display is Total: 7.50, but the total variable still holds the number 7.5.
A program that combines strip, len, upper, [::-1] and an empty-string check. Length: 6, Upper: PYTHON, Reverse: nohtyP, First: P.

conditionals.summary: Run and check the order of execution of if / else, the difference between an elif chain and separate if statements, a nested condition that prevents division by zero, input validation, and a discount condition bug caused by misusing or, together with its fix. At the end, run the grade classifier (the solution to Session 2, Lab 2).
steps: Exactly one of if and else runs. With 17 you get Under 18, with 18 you get Adult, and Start and Done, outside the indentation, are always printed.
Two separate if statements each check their own condition, so both A and B are printed. The elif chain stops at A, the first match.
The nested condition from the slides is saved as /tmp/divide.py and run twice. 7, 0 gives Cannot divide by zero; -6, 4 gives Negative result followed by Result: -1.50.
Validate first and put the normal processing inside else. The three cases, negative, zero and positive, each give a different message.
The bug from the debugging exercise: even adult gets the discount, 80.0. The "senior" on the right of or is a non-empty string, so it is always true.
Comparing both sides with customer == gives adult 100, student 80.0, senior 80.0.
"False" is also a non-empty string, so it is True. Only the empty string is False.
An elif chain that checks the highest threshold first. After Score: you get B, A, F.
